ABSTRACT
This study addresses the high time, material, and labor costs associated with the non-automated online 
parameter optimization calibration of fuel cell systems. An adaptive response surface method (ARSM) is pro -
posed to automate the calibration process and significantly reduce these costs. The low-pressure fuel cell system 
is modeled using the lumped parameter approach, including segmented models for stack channels, with opti -
mization parameters and constraints analyzed comprehensively. The ARSM algorithm dynamically shrinks the 
parameter search space during each iteration and employs a sample point inheritance strategy following space 
reduction, further minimizing time costs. Quantitative analysis demonstrates that the ARSM reduces calibration 
time by 31% compared to traditional RSM. Case studies reveal that as current load increases, the optimal oxygen 
excess ratio rises, while the optimal stack temperature declines. Latin hypercube sampling is identified as more 
efficient than full factorial sampling, and initializing optimization with the previous condition ’ s optimal values is 
shown to outperform using the parameter space center point. The proposed methodology not only enhances the 
efficiency of the calibration process but also offers a scalable and practical solution for real-time applications. 
These findings provide a robust framework for reducing costs and improving efficiency in fuel cell system 
parameter optimization.
Introduction
Background
Proton exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs) are ideal for trans -
portation and stationary power due to zero emissions, high efficiency, 
low noise, and versatile energy sources [1] . For optimal power genera -
tion, fuel cells must operate under appropriate conditions, which not 
only improve the stack ’ s performance but also extend its service life [2] . 
Consequently, many researchers have been exploring methods to 
quickly and accurately determine the optimal operating parameters 
under specific conditions.
Fuel cell parameter optimization can be conducted online for further 
control strategies or management development [3] , or offline, where the 
optimization results are used to guide fuel cell development and 
manufacturing [4] . For offline optimization, a simulation model of the 
fuel cell system is first developed. These models can vary widely, 
including dynamic simulation models [5] , computational fluid dy -
namics models [6] , or neural network models [7 – 9] . Various optimiza -
tion algorithms are employed to solve for the optimal performance 
indices. While offline methods allow complex algorithms and high ac -
curacy, model mismatch or changing conditions may reduce real-world 
applicability. In engineering, determining the optimal operating condi -
tions typically involves:adjusting the parameters manually, system sta -
bilization, data recording and repeating the process. This method, 
known as parameter calibration, is classified as an offline operation 
since the optimized results are not applied to further control or man -
agement strategy development. This calibration process is not auto -
mated, resulting in significant time, manpower, and resource costs [10] . 
Therefore, research on automated fuel cell parameter calibration and

Research status
Currently, research on fuel cell parameter optimization primarily 
focuses on optimizing either the operating parameters or the structural 
parameters of fuel cell stacks to guide stack design. The main algorithms 
can be divided into two categories: gradient-based search algorithms 
[11] and stochastic search methods, with the latter gaining increasing 
popularity in recent years. Among stochastic methods, the most 
commonly used methods include non-dominated sorting genetic algo -
rithm (NSGA) [12–17] and particle swarm optimization (PSO) [18–21] , 
alongside other optimization approaches [22] . A detailed introduction 
to the literature is listed in Table 1 .
NSGA explores solution spaces via crossover and mutation, while 
PSO guides particles toward better populations, effectively addressing 
nonlinear, multi-modal, high-dimensional problems. However, both 
face notable limitations: slow convergence, heavy reliance on initial 
population size, and extensive parameter tuning (e.g., population size, 
crossover, mutation rates for NSGA, and particle size, inertia weight, 
learning factors for PSO). Larger populations further slow convergence, 
increasing trial-and-error costs. Both are also prone to overfitting and 
premature convergence, especially when overly tied to initial favorable 
populations. In contrast, adaptive response surface method (ARSM) vi -
sualizes optimization objectives through quadratic model fitting, 
simplifying complex problems for efficient solving using established 
techniques [28] . It combines sampling, fitting, and optimization to 
accurately predict optimal values while reducing computational time. 
By iteratively shrinking the search space, ARSM accelerates convergence 
and mitigates risks of local optima. For real-time tasks where minimizing 
trial-and-error costs is critical, ARSM offers a superior alternative. 
Relevant applications of RSM in fuel cell optimization are listed in 
Table 1 .
RSM is widely applied in industry. Keshtegar et al. [29] combined 
adaptive methods with harmony search for aircraft stiffened panels, 
improving weight and buckling load predictions while enabling fast 
optimization. Long et al. [30] applied adaptive strategies with intelli -
gent space exploration to optimize hypersonic vehicles, enhancing 
global convergence, efficiency, and robustness for high-dimensional 
designs. A trust region-assisted approach improved airfoil aero -
dynamic optimization by integrating gradient-free sampling and Latin 
hypercube schemes [31] . Vafaeesefat et al. [32] optimized composite 
pressure vessels, achieving higher accuracy and reduced computational 
time via iterative design space refinement. Shi et al. [33] introduced 
reliability-based optimization for complex systems, improving sensi -
tivity estimates and designs. Egorov-Yegorov et al. [34] optimized heat- 
resistant alloys, increasing reliability and efficiency while minimizing 
experiments. These studies demonstrate adaptability and effectiveness 
in industrial optimization.
Moreover, research on the application of optimization algorithms for 
the online optimization of fuel cells primarily focuses on online energy 
management strategy development and the online estimation of model 
parameters. For example, researchers use optimization algorithms to 
determine parameters that achieve optimal energy distribution princi -
ples, thereby developing energy management strategies, as seen in 
[3,35] . Besides, research on online parameter estimation aims to 
enhance model accuracy and predictive capabilities, as demonstrated in 
[36,37] .
Contribution and organization
Based on the literature review, it is evident that research on the 
optimal parameter calibration of fuel cells is currently insufficient. 
Traditional parameter calibration methods involve not only high labor- 
and time-intensive but also exhibit inefficient in achieving optimal 
parameter calibration. This study addresses this issue by creatively 
combining the RSM algorithm with engineering problems. Furthermore, 
an ARSM approach is introduced, effectively solving various challenges 
encountered during parameter calibration and minimizing calibration 
costs. Although the focus of this study is on a 2 dimensional optimization 
problem, the proposed methodology is broadly applicable and can be 
extended to all parameter optimization and calibration problems.
The rest of this study is structured as follows: Second 2 presents the 
modeling methods for the fuel cell system. Section 3 details the appli -
cation of the ARSM algorithm in fuel cell systems. Section 4 summarizes 
and analyzes the conclusions of the parameter optimization calibration.

Methods
The low-pressure fuel cell system
The low-pressure fuel cell system, as illustrated in Fig. 1 , primarily 
consists of a stack, air supply subsystem, hydrogen supply subsystem, 
and thermal management subsystem [38] . The introduction of the 
characteristics of low-pressure fuel cell system has been provided in the 
supplementary materials .
Due to the numerous components in the low-pressure fuel cell sys -
tem, this study employs the resistance-cavity lumped parameter 
modeling method to describe the dynamic process of flows within each 
component [39] . Four assumptions were made regarding the modeling 
process. The reasonableness of these assumptions and the cavity- 
resistance modeling methods are provided in the supplementary mate -
rials . The models of each subsystem are provided in Appendix A.
Optimization variables analysis
The selection of optimization variables in this study considers both 
parameter controllability during calibration and their impact on system 
performance. Detailed principles are provided in the supplementary 
materials .
In this study, humidity is treated as a constraint within the optimi -
zation process. Based on existing fuel cell literature on humidity con -
straints [40] , the relative humidity in the cathode channels is restricted 
to a range of 58.14 % to 100 %, corresponding to membrane water 
contents of 4 and 14, respectively. A water content of 4 represents the 
upper region (nearer to the cathode side), where the membrane is drier, 
while a content of 14 corresponds to the lower region, where flooding is 
more likely to occur.
Although the cathode channel humidity constraints are defined, 
relying solely on the dehumidifier is insufficient to achieve consistent 
humidity control across all operating conditions. Therefore, this study 
employs a ’ reverse solving ’ method to determine temperature con -
straints under humidity limits, as shown in Fig. S4 . The figure depicts the 
upper and lower temperature limits required to maintain appropriate 
stack humidity at different current and OER (with perspective projection 
applied to visualize the lower surface).
From Fig. S4 , it can be observed that as the current increases and 
OER decreases, both the upper and lower bounds of temperature con -
straints increase. The space enclosed between the lower and upper 
surfaces represents the feasible temperature space that ensures adher -
ence to humidity constraints.

Sampling methods
From the principles of RSM, the accuracy of the response surface 
heavily relies on the design of sample points. An optimal sampling 
strategy should maximize response accuracy while minimizing the 
number of sample points to reduce computational costs. Generally, 
sampling methods include full factorial design, fractional factorial 
design, central composite design, and Latin hypercube design [41] . In 
this study, a comparative analysis of the full factorial design and Latin 
hypercube design is conducted.
Theoretically, increasing the number of sampling points improves 
the approximation of the real system. However, this also significantly 
increases experimental and computational costs. Full factorial design 
employs a comprehensive sampling strategy by evenly dividing each 
design interval into multiple levels, using the vertices at the in -
tersections of these levels as sample points. This approach ensures that 
the sampling points are evenly distributed across the entire design space. 
However, the number of sample points grows exponentially with 
dimensionality as l
n
, where l is the number of levels per parameter, and n 
is the problem dimension. In this study, the number of sample points in 
the full factorial design is set to 9.
In contrast, Latin hypercube design achieves high response surface 
accuracy with fewer sample points by strategically distributing the 
points to cover the design space effectively. The number of sampling 
points is set to 6 in in this study.
Given the trade-offs between computational cost and response sur -
face accuracy, this study conducted a comparative analysis of the two 
sampling methods in terms of their optimization performance and time 
cost. The findings from this analysis are provided in the Case Study 
section, providing a clear assessment of the method most suitable for the 
given optimization problem.
ARSM for parameter optimization calibration
The flowchart for parameter calibration of low-pressure fuel cell 
systems using the ARSM is shown in Fig. 2 . The process consists of the 
following steps:
1. Define the initial parameter space and select initial points. Sample 
within this space using the method outlined in Section 3.3.
2. Apply constraints to the sampled points and input them into the 
established model based on specific rules. If points from the previous 
iteration are inherited, they are not re-entered. Run the model and check 
system stability. If unstable, continue running; otherwise, record the 
response values until all are obtained.
3. Fit the response surface and optimize to find the optimal solution. 
Run the model to obtain the actual response value at this optimal point.
4. Check for convergence. If criteria are met, proceed to Step 5. If not, 
reduce the parameter space according to specific rules, record the 
relevant sample points and response values, and perform new Latin 
hypercube sampling in the updated space, returning to Step 2.
5. Verify if all predefined operating conditions have been covered. If 
so, stop the process. If not, move to the next condition, reset the 
parameter space, select an initial point based on predefined rules, and 
return to Step 2.
It is worth noting that there are still some issues in the aforemen -
tioned algorithm, including the rules for outputting sample points, 
criteria for determining system stability, constraints on sample points, 
rules for shrinking parameter space, rules for selecting initial points, and 
rules for resampling in new parameter spaces. These will be explained in 
detail below.
（ 1 ） Rules for outputting sample points.
Due to the large time constant in controlling stack temperature 
compared to the OER, the output order of a set of sample points in each 
iteration follows the following rule: sample points are outputted in 
ascending order of temperature to avoid the time cost associated with 
repeated temperature fluctuations.
（ 2 ） Criteria for determining system stability.
Whenever the ARSM outputs a sample point, the system controller 
stabilizes the system in this state and then obtains the response values of 
the sample points. In this study, the criteria for determining system 
stability are as follows. First, the data of fuel cell stack temperature, 
OER, and voltage are filtered. Then, the deviations between the actual 
values of temperature and OER and their reference values fall within a 
certain range. Finally, the fluctuations of temperature, OER, and stack 
voltage over a certain period are less than a specified value, as shown in

（ 3 ） Constraints on sample points.
The SQP algorithm ensures that the optimal solution at each iteration 
remains within the constraint boundaries. However, in subsequent 
iteration, the new sampling points may not fully lie within the updated 
parameter space. Therefore, it is necessary to check if each sample point 
satisfies the constraints. The method for checking and handling non- 
compliance with constraints is as follows. First, verify if the OER 
meets the constraints. If not, select the point within the constraint range 
that is closest to the sampled OER value. Next, consult a table to obtain 
the temperature constraint range according to Fig. S4 , and check if the 
sampling temperature satisfies the temperature constraint. If not, select

（ 4 ） Rules for shrinking parameter space.
For nonlinear optimization problems, especially those with large 
parameter spaces, traditional RSM often yield low accuracy, resulting in 
significant discrepancies between the optimal solution of the response 
surface and the optimal solution of the actual problem. Furthermore, 
different choices of initial points can lead to variations in optimization 
outcomes. Therefore, referencing the findings of Wang et al. [41] , an 
ARSM algorithm with progressively shrinking parameter space is 
employed to avoid local optima. Additionally, utilizing inheritance rules 
of sample points helps reduce the time cost of optimization problems. 
Unlike previous studies, this study progressively reduces the parameter 
space by a fixed ratio, rather than introducing two additional optimi -
zation problems [41] .
（ 5 ） Rules for selecting initial points.
The selection of initial points significantly impacts the optimization 
results and computational cost. This study aimed to optimize the oper -
ating parameters of a low-pressure fuel cell system at current loads of 
50A, 100A, 150A, 200A, 250A, and 285A. Two methods for determining 
initial points were evaluated: (1) selecting the center point of the current 
parameter space, and (2) using the optimal value from the previous 
operating condition as the initial point for the next condition. For the 
first operating condition (50A), the initial point was set to the center of 
the solution space due to the lack of prior reference points, to ensure 
efficient optimization and reduce search time.
Regarding the Latin hypercube sampling initial values described in 
Section 3.3, the same second strategy was applied, whereby the optimal 
value of the prior condition serves as the initial point for the subsequent 
condition. Sampling space boundaries were defined by operational 
constraints on OER and temperature. Specifically, the lower OER limit 
was set to 1.5, an empirical value below which oxygen starvation may 
occur in the fuel cell stack. The upper OER limit was the minimum of 
either the maximum blower flow rate (calculated as OER) or the 
empirical value of 6, which avoids unnecessary energy consumption and 
excessive water removal. The temperature bounds for each current 
condition were derived based on Fig. S4 . Thus, the sampling space for 
the Latin hypercube method was comprehensively defined.
（ 6 ） Rules for resampling in new parameter spaces.
To minimize the time cost of optimization parameter calibration, it is 
advantageous to fully utilize each sample point. After shrinking the 
parameter space, some sampling points obtained from the previous 
iteration may fall into the updated parameter space. These sample points 
can be inherited into the next batch of sample points, supplemented by 
additional sampling points through Latin hypercube sampling, thereby 
forming a new set of sampling points [41] . The specific steps are illus -
trated in Fig. 3 .
In Fig. 3 , the blue box represents the parameter space from the 
previous iteration, and the black dots or hollow points represent the 
sampling points of this iteration. The green box represents the parameter 
space for the next iteration, reduced in size compared to the blue box 
and centered around the optimal solution identified in the previous 
iteration. From Fig. 3 (a), three points fall within the parameter space of 
the next iteration. These three inherited points should be included in the 
sampling points of the next iteration. Additionally, the rows and col -
umns corresponding to the green box, where these three inherited points 
are located, are removed, resulting in an empty 3*3 box on the right side 
of Fig. 3 (a). Then, Latin hypercube sampling is conducted within this 
empty box, and the new sampling points are filled into the green box in 
order. All the circle hollow points compose the set of sampling points for 
the next iteration.
For the specific case shown in Fig. 3 (b), where two inherited sample 
points fall within the same row or column of the new parameter space, 
an additional step is required in the Latin hypercube sampling process. 
In addition to sampling within the remaining three rows or columns, a 
random point is selected from the last row or column. This results in four 
new sample points, forming a new set of seven sampling points.
Results
Selection of adaptive coefficient
To determine the adaptive contraction coefficient, this study exam -
ines the performance of the ARSM under load conditions of 150A and 
200A with various adaptive coefficients. Fig. S6 shows the efficiency 
convergence curves under different adaptive coefficients. The detailed 
efficiency, optimal OER, optimal temperature, time cost and iterations 
required are shown in Table S2 and Table S3 . It can be observed that as 
the adaptive coefficient decreases, both the optimal efficiency and the 
calibration time cost generally exhibit a declining trend. Faster 
contraction of the parameter space reduces the time cost but also de -
creases the probability of converging to the optimal solution. Addi -
tionally, large adaptive coefficients may result in a decrease in efficiency 
as the number of iterations increases (an adaptive coefficient of 0.9 
under 200A). Therefore, to balance these two metrics, this study selects 
an adaptive coefficient of 0.8.
Case study
The preset current load increases from 50A to the rated current of 
285A in increments of 50A. Subsequently, a comparative analysis of the 
parameter optimization calibration results for the following four cases is 
conducted.
Case 1: The sampling method is full factorial sampling with a sample 
size of 9 points. At each operating condition, the initial point is selected 
as the center point of the first parameter space, and the parameter space

Fig. S7 illustrates the dynamic adjustments of reference values for

Fig. S7 (a), the reference airflow decreases under high current conditions 
due to the blower ’ s maximum airflow limitation at different air pres -

current conditions compared to high current conditions, with notable 
overshoot under high current. This behavior occurs because heat gen -

whereas at high currents, significant heat generation leads to overshoot. 
Since the air flow and stack temperature control processes are similar in 
all cases, the control process diagrams for subsequent cases will not be

Case 2: At each operating condition, the initial point is selected as 
the optimal value from the previous condition. The rest of the operating 
conditions are the same as those in Case 1.
Case 3: Latin hypercube sampling is adopted in Case 3 with a sample 
size of 6 points. The other operating conditions are the same as those in 
Case 2. Difference in sampling methods results in a further reduction in 
calibration time compared to Case 2.
Case 4: Building upon Case 3, the parameter space is progressively 
reduced with a reduction ratio of 0.8, and some sampling points from the 
previous iteration are inherited using the aforementioned method for 
the next iteration. The ARSM algorithm further reduces the calibration 
time compared to Case 3.
Discussion
In Fig. 4 and Fig. 5 (a) (e), the current variations during the 
parameter calibration process are depicted. In (b), (c), and (d), the black 
lines depict the actual efficiencies corresponding to the optimal solu -
tions obtained in each iteration, optimal OER, and optimal stack tem -
perature, respectively. The blue, pink, and orange lines represent the 
optimal values of efficiency, OER, and stack temperature for each 
operating condition. The optimal values for all cases can be found in 
Table 2 . Analysis reveals that the optimization results across all cases are 
highly consistent, following the same overall trend. Notably, the graph 
indicates a one-iteration delay in the appearance of the optimal effi -
ciency, as the actual efficiency is calculated in the subsequent iteration 
based on the optimal OER and stack temperature values derived 
previously.
An obvious characteristic is that the optimal efficiency decreases 
with increasing current across operating conditions, while it generally 
improves within each current condition. However, in certain iterations, 
such as the second optimization iteration from 150A to 285A in Case 1, 
the actual efficiency decreases due to the mismatch between the 
response surface model and the actual model. This phenomenon

diminishes noticeably from Case 1 to Case 4, indicating the significant 
impact of initial point selection and sampling method on the optimiza -
tion process. It is also evident that the optimal OER decreases with 
increasing current, while the optimal stack temperature increases with 
current, akin to high-pressure fuel cell systems [4] .
Table 2 also summarizes the total calibration time cost, average 
number of iterations, and average time cost per iteration for all cases. 
Case 1 exhibits the highest average number of iterations, primarily due 
to initial points being farther from the optimal solution, leading to 
increased optimization time costs. In contrast, Case 4 demonstrates the 
lowest average optimization time per iteration, enabled by inheriting 
some sample points into subsequent iterations, thus reducing the cali -
bration time cost for parameter optimization. Under identical condi -
tions, the Latin hypercube sampling method required 1168.3 s, 
significantly less than the 1627.6 s of the full factorial method. Despite 
using fewer sample points, the Latin hypercube approach maintained 
comparable accuracy while reducing computational time, demon -
strating its efficiency and suitability for time-constrained optimization 
problems. Moreover, the strategy of selecting the optimal value from the 
previous condition as the initial point for the next condition proves su -
perior to using the center point of the parameter space as the initial 
point. Additionally, the ARSM approach outperforms the conventional 
RSM by leveraging inherited sampling points to significantly reduce the 
number of new points required in each iteration, thereby lowering

6.Conclusion
This study presents a novel approach for automating the parameter 
optimization calibration process of low-pressure fuel cells, addressing 
the addressing the high resource costs of manual calibration. By 
leveraging the resistance-cavity lumped parameter modeling method, 
comprehensive models were developed for the various subsystems of the 
fuel cell, along with a segmented lumped parameter model for the stack 
channels. The primary contribution of this work is the application of an 
ARSM algorithm to streamline and automate the fuel cell calibration 
process. The ARSM algorithm iteratively reduces the parameter space, 
significantly decreasing the time costs associated with the optimization 
process. In addition, the inheritance of sample points following sample 
space reduction further optimizes time efficiency. Comparative analysis 
revealed that the ARSM outperforms the traditional RSM by reducing 
time costs by 31 %. Key findings from the study include:
1. As the current load increases, the required optimal OER also in -
creases, while the optimal stack temperature decreases.
2. Using the optimal values from the previous optimization iteration 
as the initial point for the next iteration results in a reduced time cost 
compared to using the parameter space center point.
3. Latin hypercube sampling proves more efficient than full factorial 
sampling in reducing the time cost of parameter optimization 
calibration.
4. The ARSM algorithm, incorporating sample point inheritance, 
further enhances efficiency and reduces time costs.
These findings highlight both the effectiveness of the proposed 
methodology and its potential for real-time applications in fuel cell 
systems. This research represents a significant advancement in opti -
mizing fuel cell parameter calibration and offers substantial improve -
ments in reducing operational costs.
In future work, the proposed automated parameter optimization 
calibration method will be extended to high-pressure fuel cell systems. 
However, this expansion introduces several new challenges. First, a 
greater number of optimization parameters must be considered, such as 
cathode inlet air pressure, OER, stack outlet temperature, stack 
inlet – outlet temperature difference, hydrogen excess ratio, and oper -
ating current density. Second, control challenges become more pro -
nounced in high-pressure systems, encompassing temperature 
regulation, humidity management, decoupled control of air pressure 
and mass flow rate, and precise hydrogen pressure regulation. Accurate 
parameter control is a prerequisite for automatic calibration. Addition -
ally, as the dimensionality of the optimization problem grows, compu -
tational real-time demands increase, necessitating the development of 
suboptimal solution strategies. Furthermore, optimization strategies 
must be tailored to address non-standard operating conditions, such as 
cold-start processes or energy recovery mechanisms in air supply com -
ponents. These challenges will require further research and adjustments 
to the proposed methodology for successful application in high-pressure 
fuel cell systems.
